what: Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) in London ran its first computer match-ups of questionnaire answers on a time-shared computer.

sources.title: Joan Ball
sources.quote: the bureau ran its first set of computer match ups in 1964.

sources.title: Operation Match
sources.quote: inspired by Joan Ball's St. James Computer Dating Service (later Com-Pat) which started in London in 1964.

note: Considered Operation Match (1965, later), the Scientific Marriage Foundation (1957, IBM card-sorting machine, not a computer, so rejected) and unnamed earlier European computer dating services that Wikipedia says preceded both Com-Pat and Operation Match; I could not identify or date them, so an earlier event may exist. Demonstration and first service are the same event.

sources.title: Joan Ball

what: John Horty's Health Law Center at the University of Pittsburgh built a computer database of statutes searchable by computer, shown to the American Bar Association in 1960.

sources.title: University of Pittsburgh School of Law
sources.quote: During the 1950s and 1960s, the School of Law's Health Law Center was an early pioneer in the field now known as computer-assisted legal research

note: The fetched page says only 1950s-60s; the 1960 ABA demonstration year comes from a search-result snippet I could not fetch (non-Wikipedia sites were blocked by the proxy). Only the legal-research part of the definition is real; no computer issues verdicts or warrants.

what: Mead Data Central publicly launched LEXIS in New York as a commercial computerized legal research service for lawyers.

sources.title: LexisNexis
sources.quote: On April 2, 1973, MDC publicly launched LEXIS at a press conference in New York City

note: Earlier candidates: Horty's Pittsburgh system (1960s) and the Ohio Bar's OBAR (contract 1967, per the same article), which were in use before LEXIS but whose first service dates I could not source. LEXIS is the first commercial end-user service. No verdict or sentencing milestone exists.

what: The FBI's National Crime Information Center, a computerized national database of wanted persons and stolen property, was created.

sources.title: National Crime Information Center
sources.quote: The NCIC database was created in 1967 under FBI director J. Edgar Hoover.

note: Loose fit: NCIC looks up records to find wanted people but does not analyse evidence or predict crime. Search results suggested city police computers (e.g. St. Louis, c.1965) pre-date NCIC but I could not fetch a source. PredPol (2011) is a later, predictive-policing event; no earlier predictive milestone was verified.

what: IBM mechanized voting and ballot tabulation for single transferable vote elections, with voters recording preferences on punched cards by dial machine.

sources.title: Voting machine
sources.quote: By July 1936, IBM had mechanized voting and ballot tabulation for single transferable vote elections.

note: Electromechanical rather than computer; whether it was used in a real election is not stated. Considered Edison's 1869 electric vote recorder and legislative electric roll-call devices but could not source them. Lever machines (1892) and McTammany punched-paper machines (1890s) are mechanical, so rejected.

what: Seven US counties switched to punched-card voting with computer tallying for the 1964 presidential election.

sources.title: Electronic voting
sources.quote: Their first widespread use was in the US where 7 counties switched to this method for the 1964 presidential election.

note: The Voting machine article dates the Votomatic's first major success to 1965; the Electronic voting article says 1964. Earlier small-scale uses may exist.

what: By the 1996 US presidential election punched-card systems with computer tabulation were used by over a third of registered US voters.

sources.title: Voting machine
sources.quote: By the 1996 Presidential election, some variation of the punched card system was used by 37.3% of registered voters in the United States.

note: US-only figure; the share may have exceeded this or been similar earlier. Brazil and India adopted DRE machines nationally later.

what: Harvard researchers (the Schwitzgebel brothers) developed portable transceivers that recorded the location of volunteers.

sources.title: Electronic tagging
sources.quote: Portable transceivers that could record the location of volunteers were first developed by a group of researchers at Harvard University in the early 1960s.

note: Source gives only 'early 1960s'; 1962 is a midpoint, not a sourced year. The first pass said 1964, unverified. Vehicle-tracking and animal/astronaut telemetry were not examined.

what: Judge Jack Love persuaded Michael Goss to found NIMCOS, which built radio ankle transmitters used to monitor offenders from a telephone-linked receiver.

sources.title: Electronic tagging
sources.quote: in 1982, an Arizona state district judge, Jack Love, convinced a former sales representative of Honeywell Information Systems, Michael T. Goss

note: The page gives 1982 for the company; the first pass said the first tagged probationer was in April 1983 (New Mexico), which I could not source. The Schwitzgebel 1960s system was a research use with volunteers.

what: IBM developed a way of attaching magnetic stripes to plastic cards under a US government contract for a security system.

sources.title: Magnetic stripe card
sources.quote: In 1960, IBM built upon the magnetic tape idea and developed a reliable way of securing magnetic stripes to plastic cards

note: The same article says Forrest Parry had the idea in 1969, so 1960 conflicts with it. Punched-card key systems and earlier access cards were not checked.

what: Tor Sornes's recodable punched plastic keycard lock, the VingCard, was used in hotels.

sources.title: Keycard lock
sources.quote: Tor Sørnes was credited with the invention in the 1970s.

note: Page gives only the 1970s; 1975 is from the first pass (single source). Hand-geometry Identimat with a magnetic-card reader (1970s) and 1960s card-access systems (e.g. Cardkey) may be earlier but were not sourced.

what: J. H. Wegstein at the US National Bureau of Standards developed computer models of fingerprints to automate their analysis, leading to AFIS.

sources.title: Identix Incorporated
sources.quote: In the 1960s, J. H. Wegstein at the National Bureau of Standards developed computer models for fingerprint representations

note: Source gives only 'the 1960s'; 1965 is a midpoint, not sourced. Identimat is hand geometry, so rejected. Search results indicate the FBI asked NBS for help in 1963 and Rockwell built card readers from 1974, but I could not fetch these. 1999 IAFIS is a database, not the earliest.

what: Apple introduced Touch ID fingerprint unlocking on the iPhone 5s, putting fingerprint readers in millions of ordinary phones.

sources.title: Touch ID
sources.quote: the iPhone 5s was unveiled on September 10, 2013, and was the first phone on a major US carrier to feature the technology.

note: Introduction year, not a measured adoption figure; use is routine on phones from about 2013 to 2015.

what: John Daugman patented and published the first working iris-recognition algorithms and gave the first live demonstrations.

sources.title: Iris recognition
sources.quote: In 1994 he patented this basis for iris recognition and its underlying computer vision algorithms for image processing

note: Flom and Safir's 1980s patent on the concept had no working algorithm, so rejected. Retina scanning is older: EyeDentify was formed in 1976 and a scanner concept emerged in 1975 (Retinal scan article), but I found no dated working demonstration, so no retina milestone is given.

what: Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located facial features and measured ratios without human intervention.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In 1970, Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located anatomical features such as the chin

note: Bledsoe, Chan and Bisson (1964-65) needed a human to mark feature coordinates, so rejected as semi-automated; the earlier system did the matching by computer, so a looser reading would date the demonstration to 1964-65.

what: The Mexican government used face recognition software to detect duplicate voter registrations for the 2000 presidential election.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In the 2000 Mexican presidential election, the Mexican government employed face recognition software to prevent voter fraud.

note: The same article says West Virginia and New Mexico DMV offices were first to use it after 1993 (undated), so an earlier use likely exists. Super Bowl XXXV (2001) is later.

what: Apple announced Face ID on the iPhone X, bringing face recognition to ordinary phone unlocking.

sources.title: Face ID
sources.quote: Apple announced Face ID alongside the iPhone X on September 12, 2017

note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure.

what: LEO I at J. Lyons and Co. ran the first business application on a computer.

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: LEO I ran its first business application in 1951.

note: Mechanical tabulators and accounting machines (from the 1890s) do clerical work; I treated the concept as electronic/computer clerical work and did not research them. Payroll dates (1951 vs 1953) conflict across sources.

what: LEO I did real clerical work for Lyons (bakery valuations, later payroll and invoicing).

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: LEO I ran its first business application in 1951.

note: Same event as the demonstration, in service for Lyons's own business.

what: The NSA/GCHQ ECHELON network was formally established to intercept satellite communications and screen them by keyword.

sources.title: Echelon (signals intelligence)
sources.quote: the ECHELON project became formally established in 1971.

sources.title: Echelon (signals intelligence)
sources.quote: US intelligence uses interception systems and keyword searches to monitor European businesses.

note: Weak fit: sources describe keyword screening, not transcription of speech. SHAMROCK (1945-75) handled telegrams largely by hand, so rejected. I found no source for earlier automated speech screening.

concept_note: First pass said Operation Match 1965; Joan Ball's 1964 London service is earlier, and unnamed earlier European services are reported. No mass adoption established.

No milestone: the first pass had only CAT-ASVAB (1996), which I could not source with a quote and which is a loose fit; I could not find or fetch sources for earlier computerized selection (e.g. US Employment Service job banks, 1968, seen only in snippets).
Added Horty's earlier 1960 demonstration (low confidence). LEXIS 1973 kept as first commercial service. Nothing decides verdicts or sentences.

Added NCIC 1967 as an earlier, loose-fitting computerized police record system; the 2011 PredPol event is not given because the page lacks a quote for it. Earlier police computers exist but were not sourced.
Went earlier than the first pass's 1964: IBM's 1936 punched-card STV voting machine (low confidence). 1964 counties kept as first practical use; 1996 punched-card share for mass adoption.
No milestone, as in the first pass. Norwegian (1964) and other Nordic population registers are computerized registers but not dossiers that track citizens; I could not source a fit.
Added ECHELON 1971 as a low-confidence practical use; no earlier automated speech screening found. No demonstration milestone.

Dated the Harvard demonstration to the early 1960s (earlier than the first pass's 1964 guess); the practical-use date is the 1982 NIMCOS company, not the 1983 first wearer, because only 1982 could be sourced.
Kept the first pass's 1960 magstripe and 1975 VingCard dates but both are low confidence; 1970s card-access systems were not checked.

Dropped the 1999 IAFIS practical use as the wrong kind of event; added the 1960s NBS demonstration (year uncertain). Earliest practical use (FBI/Rockwell 1970s, fingerprint locks) could not be sourced.
Kept the 1994 iris demonstration; dropped the 1995 practical use (no fetchable source). Retina scanning has no dated demonstration found.
First pass gave 1965 semi-automated; I moved the demonstration to Kanade's 1970 fully automatic system and added 2000 practical use and 2017 phone adoption.
No milestones: the first pass's Bell Labs 1964 work and TI early-1970s system could not be fetched, and the pages I could read give only much later dates.
Treated as electronic clerical work; LEO 1951 kept for both kinds and 1953 payroll left aside. No mass adoption: word processing term appeared only in the early 1970s.
No milestone: a social condition, not a device or event with a date.
